title: 3 lessons from rebuilding Atlassian’s product development lifecycle for people and agents
summary: AI makes execution faster. Improving the entire PDLC requires evolving the way teams work together.
body_markdown:
### Written by:[Avani Prabhakar](https://www.atlassian.com/blog/author/avani-prabhakar)


Chief People and AI Enablement Officer


AI has made it easier than ever to build software. But that doesn’t mean teams have become better at building products.


Our[2026 State of Developer Experience](https://www.atlassian.com/teams/software-development/state-of-developer-experience-2026) research shows why. In 2025, 68% of developers said AI saved them 10+ hours a week. This year, just 26% do, and 49% now spend four or more hours a week managing AI. When agents can generate code, designs, and prototypes in minutes, the bottleneck moves to deciding what’s worth building and whether it’s good enough.


**Building better products won’t come from AI alone. We need to rethink how product, design, and engineering work together, and how people and agents turn ideas into customer value.**


Across the industry, product, design, and engineering teams are redesigning how they work with AI, but largely in silos. At Atlassian, we’re taking on the bigger challenge of transforming the entire product development lifecycle (PDLC).


This is no small undertaking. We have nearly 10,000 R&D employees, and we’re testing new ways of working across both greenfield projects and complex legacy systems with strict security and compliance requirements. We’re sharing what we’ve learned so our customers can navigate these same challenges and accelerate their own AI transformations.


As the teamwork company, we believe the biggest opportunity lies in the messy middle: where work moves between disciplines, context gets shared, and human judgment matters most. That’s where we’re focusing our AI-first PDLC experiments.


We’ve captured our experiments, results, and three guiding principles in the[Atlassian AI PDLC Playbook](https://atlassian.com/blog/guides-research/ai-product-development-lifecycle-playbook) :


1. **Aim human attention where it changes the outcome.** Let agents handle repetitive work while people focus on consequential decisions.
2. **Context should travel with the work – and compound.** Connect knowledge across people, agents, and tools so every stage builds on what came before.
3. **Widen contribution, protect craft accountability and ambition.** Broaden who can contribute while keeping experts accountable for quality.


Here’s what each one looks like in practice.


## Learning 1: Aim human attention where it changes the outcome


Agents can now execute work faster than people can review it. That raises a critical question: *Where does judgment make the biggest difference?*


At Atlassian, we’re redesigning workflows so people don’t have to supervise every step an agent takes. Instead, humans focus on the moments when their expertise changes the outcome.


Take security vulnerabilities. Our scanners used to flag issues that engineers then had to investigate and fix, often spending hours on work that followed predictable patterns. Across thousands of repositories, that added up.


Today, agents do much of that work first. An automated pipeline identifies vulnerabilities, proposes fixes, and runs tests before an engineer gets involved. Instead of starting with an alert, engineers start with a proposed solution and decide whether it’s safe to ship.


**Agents now prepare fixes for 52% of vulnerabilities, saving roughly 50 engineering days a week.**


For engineers, this changes the job itself. They spend less time investigating routine issues and more time applying their expertise to the decisions that matter. And for leaders like me, it reinforces that we need to redesign roles and expectations around where human judgment creates value, not simply add AI to existing workflows.


## Learning 2: Context should travel with the work — and compound


AI lets people and agents work across the traditional stages of product development, often simultaneously. We now need to figure out: *How do we keep everyone working from the same understanding?*


Agents can build at incredible speed. But without the right context, they can build the wrong thing before anyone has a chance to course-correct.


Consider how product requirements traditionally move through development. A PM defines what to build, designers refine the experience, and engineers turn those decisions into code. Along the way, important context can get lost, forcing each new contributor to reconstruct what others already knew.


We’re changing that through spec-driven development. Teams work with AI to define what to build and how to build it, capturing those decisions in shared specifications that people can review and refine. Those same specifications become Jira tasks that agents execute and update. Instead of starting over at every handoff, people and agents build on the same evolving understanding.


**In one Confluence pilot, engineers shipped two production features in 2 and 4 developer weeks, compared with historical estimates of 30 and 40 weeks.**


This is one of the most important people implications of AI. When decisions and reasoning live only in people’s heads, knowledge gets lost as teams change. When we capture and maintain that context in the systems where work happens, every new teammate — human or agent — can start further ahead.


## Learning 3: Widen contribution, protect craft accountability and ambition


AI separates the ability to produce work from the expertise needed to evaluate it. Which raises the question: *How do we expand who can contribute while continuing to raise the bar for quality?*


AI makes it possible for PMs to prototype, designers to write code, and agents to contribute across disciplines. But being able to *generate* something isn’t the same as knowing whether it’s good. Deep expertise in product, design, and engineering becomes more important, not less.


Consider how small product improvements traditionally get made. A PM or designer identifies an issue, defines the change, and hands it to engineering for implementation. Even straightforward fixes depend on someone else to build them.


We’re changing that. Through an internal initiative, PMs and designers who had never written production code used AI to take small customer-facing improvements all the way to production. Engineers helped scope the changes, reviewed the code, and upheld technical standards.


**In just three months, more than 50 PMs and designers shipped over 100 engineering-approved production changes.**


But to be clear, the opportunity in the AI era isn’t more people building more things. It’s to bring expert judgment into more of the work and creating a shared language where multidisciplinary teams can reach better outcomes, faster.


This also changes how we think about people’s roles. At Atlassian, we’re approaching that shift in a deliberate order: tasks first, skills second, roles third. Understand how AI changes the work, then what skills people need, and only then how roles should evolve. Deep expertise doesn’t disappear; its impact grows.


## Redesign the system, not just the toolset


My advice to leaders: don’t look at individual jobs to be done in the PDLC and simply add AI. Look at the handoffs between product, design, and engineering, and at how AI can help you reduce friction across them. The biggest opportunity is redesigning how disciplines work together.


The companies that lead the next era of product development won’t be those generating the most code or deploying the most agents. They’ll be the ones whose teams can turn ideas into customer value most effectively, with a system that gets smarter every cycle.


Read the full[Atlassian AI PDLC Playbook](https://atlassian.com/blog/guides-research/ai-product-development-lifecycle-playbook) for every example, the results behind them, and practical guidance for redesigning your own PDLC.
